extracted.intended_audience: students learning creative writing (middle/high school English students)
extracted.subtask_description: Instructional guidance on converting 'telling' sentences into vivid 'showing' sentences for fiction and narrative writing, with examples and student exercises. Focuses on sentence- and scene-level techniques to create sensory, action-driven prose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show, Don't Tell (overall principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: The single best piece of advice: 'Don't tell me, show me.' Don't tell the reader a fact about a character or scene (e.g., 'the character is angry'); show it through action, sensory detail, and dialogue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Called 'The First Rule of Writing' in this packet. The right way is to 'show' information through the use of action, dialogue, and the five senses. Examples throughout the packet transform simple telling sentences into showing sentences to illustrate the principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish telling sentences from showing sentences
rubrics_metrics.description: Telling sentences give general, non-specific, often vague information and do not involve the reader; showing sentences describe scenes and actions and help the reader see by using clear, specific details.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Telling is a way of communicating facts—the wrong way. Showing dramatizes the events of your plot; the reader experiences the story as if he's right there, participating. Examples: 'Jack was afraid.' (telling) vs. a multi-sensory scene (showing).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use specific details
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific details breathe life into your story and create clear, strong pictures in the reader's mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific details stimulate the reader's imagination so he can project himself into the scene and become part of it. The packet repeatedly emphasizes replacing vague labels with concrete sensory/physical details (e.g., 'sweat chilled his palms', 'gritty bricks against his cheek').

rubrics_metrics.name: Show emotion through action, the five senses, and dialogue (avoid naming emotions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid naming emotions directly (e.g., 'Jack was afraid'); instead show the emotion by describing physical reactions, sensations, and speech.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The packet warns: 'watch out whenever you name an emotion... It's lazy writing.' Use action, the five senses, and dialogue to convey emotional states (examples show fear, anger, joy without naming them).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use action and physical behavior to reveal character and situation
rubrics_metrics.description: Reveal characters' feelings, intentions, and relationships through what they do—their gestures, movements, and interactions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Brenda slamming a drawer, hiding hands, and stammering dialogue to show secretiveness; Jim grabbing Blair and slamming him into the wall to show violence/anger. 'Give proof of how this character acts and reacts when faced by problems.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Use dialogue to show information and character
rubrics_metrics.description: Let characters' spoken words (and the way they speak) convey information, attitude, and subtext instead of exposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Packet examples use clipped or stammering dialogue to reveal emotion and motive. It also cautions to 'avoid boring dialogue' and to use dialogue as one of the main tools to 'show' rather than 'tell.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Employ the five senses to create immersive scenes
rubrics_metrics.description: Use sight, sound, smell, taste, and touch to make scenes vivid and believable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The packet instructs: 'we need to see, hear, feel, smell and taste your story.' Examples include tactile details (gritty bricks), auditory details (footsteps tapping), and visual details (mozzarella bubbling) to pull readers into the moment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatize events so the reader participates
rubrics_metrics.description: Present events as scenes that play out (like a movie) so readers live through them rather than being told facts about them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The packet uses the movie-theater metaphor: a black screen with only soundtrack is frustrating; likewise, failing to make the reader see your story causes loss of interest. 'Showing sentences dramatize the events of your plot... the reader experiences the story as if he's right there.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Use figurative language and descriptive vocabulary
rubrics_metrics.description: Enhance showing with similes, metaphors, and vivid descriptive words to paint the narrative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The packet explicitly advises to 'USE figurative language (similes and metaphors), dialogue and descriptive words.' Figurative language is presented as part of the palette for painting narrative scenes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make characters three-dimensional by proving behavior (show why readers should cheer or boo)
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide evidence of a character's qualities through their actions and reactions so readers form opinions and emotional investment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The packet: 'give proof to the reader—proof of how this character acts and reacts... you

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid vague, general statements and labeled judgments
rubrics_metrics.description: Replace generic evaluations ('the party was great', 'the book was intriguing', 'she is creative') with concrete, scene-level evidence and specifics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The student exercises list many telling sentences for conversion, demonstrating the anti-pattern of relying on labels rather than demonstrative detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice converting telling sentences into showing sentences
rubrics_metrics.description: An instructional exercise: given a telling sentence, write a showing sentence that dramatizes the idea using action, senses, and dialogue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The packet includes numerous paired examples and a long student exercise list (items 1–46 and 28–46 etc.) plus a graded writing assignment template for students to complete showing sentences corresponding to telling prompts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use memorable descriptions and avoid boring dialogue
rubrics_metrics.description: Aim for memorable descriptive passages and engaging dialogue; avoid flat or dull phrasing that fails to involve the reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The packet states: 'You have to use the senses, avoid boring dialogue, and write memorable descriptions.' This is presented as necessary to make characters and scenes stick with readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paint narrative with words (show scenes as happening now or how they happened)
rubrics_metrics.description: Present scenes either as immediate, unfolding action ('what's happening now') or as dramatized past events ('how things happened') to create narrative momentum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instruction: 'SHOW the scene, GET them involved, GIVE it a dramatic impact, SHOW them what's happening now or how things happened by painting your narrative with words.'
